thread.title: Xiaomi: The Pricing Is An Opportunity - Xiaomi (BATS:XI)

author: B&B Market
title: Xiaomi: The Pricing Is An Opportunity - Xiaomi (BATS:XI)
text:
Xiaomi ( XI ) priced on Friday and it was underwhelming to say the least. Original estimates said that the valuation would be in the $100 billion range however, the actual valuation came in at just $54 billion. With this much of a discrepancy in the valuation of the company, is there any opportunity for investors?
Listing Details Xiaomi priced its public shares on June 26, 2018 on the Hong Kong Stock Exchange at a price of HK$17 ($2.17) per share. At this price, the company expects to raise $4.7 billion, below the original target of $10 billion. The listing was expected to be the largest listing since Alibaba's (NYSE: BABA ) public offering in 2014, but because of the lower amount of raised capital, it is the largest offering on the HKEX since 2016.
Source: Crunchbase
Original estimates were pointing to a record high valuation of $100 billion. This was rolled back to a range of $60-$70 billion in early June. The actual pricing valuation was priced even lower than the lowest estimate at $54 billion, roughly half of the original amount.
Environment With such a shortcoming on the valuation, it is a clear indicator of the current state of the Chinese markets. The Shanghai Composite index has declined more than 20% since its highs in January earlier this year. Just recently, the market moved into official bear market territory, as it is now down more than 10% year-to-date. This has weighed on tech stocks, and is affecting American sentiment towards Chinese companies.
Some of the biggest names, including Alibaba, Baidu ( BIDU ), and recent IPO iQIYI ( IQ ), are feeling the pressure, as they have been on the decline over the last month.
BABA 1-Month Price Returns (Daily) data by YCharts
As we can see below, the Hang Seng Index (Hong Kong's index) has tumbled about 2000 points since the beginning of June. This equates to a 6.59% decline in a month. This is a rough environment for a company to list in, especially with the current geopolitical tensions.
Source: Google
While Trump and Xi continue to threaten tariffs back and forth, the companies affected will suffer. However, Xiaomi seems to have been caught in the crossfire. The company is not publicly trading yet as the shares open for trading on July 9, 2018. However, the market may see more trouble by then or reverse its trajectory and recover.
Valuation The Hong Kong market is a volatile market. However, around 2012, the P/E ratio began to stabilize in the 8x to 12.5x range. After dipping to a 7-year low (7.5x) in 2016, the markets have been on a rise up until this year. In early 2018, the market reached a high at 17.5x before falling off a cliff thanks to the reasons discussed above.
Source: CEIC
Xiaomi has a P/E of ~51x according to The Standard . This is very expensive compared to the Hong Kong market. Competitors of Xiaomi have much lower P/E ratios. Huawei is at 17.8x while Apple ( AAPL ), shown below, is at 15.97x.
AAPL PE Ratio (Forward) data by YCharts
However, it is important to remember that Xiaomi is a growth company, and as a result, P/E ratios are most likely not the best method to value the company, at least not yet. A better method is to forget about valuation in general and attempt to find an expected return.
First off, it is important to recognize that Xiaomi is a growing electronics stock. There can be some debate (especially today) about whether or not smartphones are considered durable or discretionary, but I will stick with the historical discretionary sector. This means that the company will not be expected to perform that strongly in the current bear market.
The average unlevered-beta for US electronics companies (out of 167 companies) is 0.91. The average levered beta is 0.94. The risk-free rate for Hong Kong would be the '10Y Hong Kong Government Bond', which yields 2.254%. Since 1988, the Hong Kong market has averaged a 10.22% return. To recap, we will do a levered and unlevered version... the formulas are as follows:
Levered:
Exp. Return = 2.254% + 0.94 (10.22% - 2.254%)
Exp. Return = 9.74%
Unlevered:
Exp. Return = 2.254% + 0.91(10.22% - 2.254%)
Exp. Return = 9.50%
This may seem like a low expected return, and it is. This is the minimum requirement without factoring in a bear market, IPO status, hype surrounding the company, growth stock, etc. All of these factors are going to alter the expected return but to what extent is up to the individual investor. For example, I added a 5% premium for a bear market and a 1.50% premium for a growth stock. This gave me an unlevered expected return of 15.42%, which may still be on the low side depending on the time horizon.
Global Expansion Xiaomi should not be as affected by the tariff war between the US and China, which boosts both its short and long-term prospectus. One reason for this is its lack of exposure to the US market. Xiaomi is a main competitor within the Chinese mainland, with a 14% market share (rank #5) as of Q4 2017.
Source: Gizmochina
However, the company is starting to decrease its reliance upon its home country. In 2017, China composed 72% of total revenues, down from 86.6% in 2016. The reason this is decreasing is because Xiaomi is making an aggressive push into international markets. Below is the market share breakdown for the Indian smartphone market. Xiaomi managed to overtake Samsung ( OTC:SSNLF ), and became the leading brand inside the country.
Source: Telecom
The company grew 155% YoY to 9.3 million shipments as of Q1'18. Samsung grew 24% YoY to 7.5 million shipments. In third and fourth was Oppo and Vivo with 2.8 and 2.1 million shipments respectively.
On top of this, the company is also planning an aggressive expansion into Europe. This expansion strategy is actually quite different than the historical growth strategy management implements. As an example, the company is looking to open 2000 physical stores (1000 domestic and 1000 abroad). Xiaomi made its way into the mainstream by selling a budget-friendly smartphone online. At the end of 2017, a few stores were opened in Spain, and have fared well according to management but there were no concrete numbers.
While there is not a clear path laid out for where the company is looking to move into, the company has quietly been making moves with its IP portfolio. The company has been involved in many patent lawsuits and understandably. Some of the smartphones look remarkably like Apple phones. However, management has been building up its patent portfolio, with over 3500 filings in 2015. The image below shows where the patents have been located.
Source: Greyb
We can conclude that the states are in the scope of the expansion strategy. There are almost double the number of patents in the US vs. Europe, but the company is already opening stores in Europe while the US is only online sales.
Along with filing for patents, there has been a rise in patent acquisition deals. One example, (and this is also a reason why the trade war won't hurt Xiaomi as much) is the acquisition of 30 patents from Leadcore Technologies. This deal allowed Xiaomi to make its own chips and other hardware parts for its phones making them the 4th phone maker in the world to do so. There have also been deals with Ninebot (who acquired Segway), Qualcomm (NASDAQ: QCOM ), Broadcom (NASDAQ: AVGO ), Intel (NASDAQ: INTC ), and many others.
The expansion is not just focused upon smartphones either. The company is also looking to ramp up its 'smart' products production. As I mentioned above, the company acquired patents from the acquisition of Segway. This applies to smart 'self-balancing' scooters and other transport methods. There are other products such as smart TVs and speakers, some of these products have seen their entire inventory wiped out just hours after release.
Conclusion Xiaomi has seen its ups and downs since forming in 2010. There was rocket-growth until stagnation in 2015, and then the company made a one-of-a-kind turnaround story to rocket-growth again in 2017. The funds raised from the public listing are going to be used to continue this strong growth by pushing into international markets. There will be less reliance (but not abandonment) of its home market in China, as the focus turns to wealthier markets such as Europe and potentially America.
There are many strengths to Xiaomi, but they are all undermined by one weakness. The company has very little 'uniqueness' to its products. The main competitive advantage is that the products are cheaper than the competition. Unless the company can continually provide cheap, quality products there is a chance the company will lose its grasp and fall back to Earth.
Disclosure: I/we have no positions in any stocks mentioned, and no plans to initiate any positions within the next 72 hours.
